body: {"total":2,"records":[{"title":"Continuity with a usual family physician and unplanned hospital admission in adults aged 65 and over: a population study","authors":"Engelbrecht-Musa R, Holloway-Nakata S, Pereira-Achebe L","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Primary Care Continuity","doi":"10.5555/jpcc.2021.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 118,000 adults aged 65 and over registered with family practices for two years, measuring continuity with a usual provider index from outpatient visits in the first year. Patients in the highest continuity quintile had fewer unplanned admissions in the second year than those in the lowest (rate ratio 0.84, 95 percent CI 0.79 to 0.90) after adjustment for age, sex, number of chronic conditions and prior admissions. The association was stronger for admissions for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions (rate ratio 0.76). Sicker patients see more physicians, so residual confounding by severity is possible despite adjustment."},{"title":"Changes in continuity after practice reorganisation and emergency admissions: an interrupted time series in 14 practices","authors":"Vasquez-Hollander T, Oyelaran-Frost M","year":2024,"venue":"Family Practice Organisation Studies","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Fourteen family practices introduced personal lists that linked each patient aged 65 and over to one physician. Over 18 months, the continuity index for these patients rose from 0.46 to 0.61. Emergency admissions among them fell by 6 percent relative to the pre-existing trend (95 percent CI -1 to 12 percent), an estimate compatible with no change. Waits for routine appointments rose from a median of 6 to 9 days. There were no comparison practices, and a regional admission avoidance scheme started during the same period."}]}
